title: Management of hyperglycemia in type 2 diabetes: a consensus algorithm for the initiation and adjustment of therapy. A consensus statement from the American Diabetes Association and the European Association for the Study of Diabetes
authors: Nathan DM, Buse JB, Davidson MB, Heine RJ, Holman RR, Sherwin R, Zinman B
funder: Funding of the consensus process is not stated in the article, which records that it was published simultaneously in Diabetes Care and Diabetologia by the American Diabetes Association and the European Association for the Study of Diabetes. Author disclosures are published in full.
authorConflicts: All seven authors declare industry relationships: research grants, advisory board membership, speakers' bureau participation or honoraria from companies including Aventis, Novo Nordisk, Amylin, Becton Dickinson, Bristol-Myers Squibb, Hoffmann-La Roche, Eli Lilly, Merck, Novartis, Pfizer, Sanofi-Aventis, GlaxoSmithKline, Minimed-Medtronic, Takeda, Merck Sante, Pronova, Johnson & Johnson and Smiths Medical.
result: This statement set the algorithm that made metformin the first drug of type 2 diabetes: the panel's consensus was that metformin therapy should be initiated concurrently with lifestyle intervention at diagnosis, recommended as initial pharmacologic therapy in the absence of specific contraindications for its effect on glycaemia, absence of weight gain or hypoglycaemia, generally low level of side effects, high acceptance and relatively low cost, and titrated to its maximally effective dose over one to two months. The authors state that the guidelines and algorithm are based on clinical trials and on the authors' clinical experience and judgment; that the paucity of high-quality evidence directly comparing treatment regimens remains a major impediment to recommending one class over another; that apart from effects on glycaemia there are insufficient data to recommend one class of glucose-lowering agent over others with regard to complications; that the UK Prospective Diabetes Study could not demonstrate clear superiority of sulphonylurea, metformin or insulin for complications; and that the beneficial effect of metformin on cardiovascular outcomes in that study needs to be confirmed. Metformin monotherapy is given as lowering HbA1c by about 1.5 percentage points, with lactic acidosis quite rare at fewer than 1 case per 100,000 treated patients. On targets, the statement records that the most recent American Diabetes Association goal, selected on the basis of practicality and the projected reduction in complications over time, is in general an HbA1c below 7%, with as close to normal as possible without significant hypoglycaemia for the individual patient, and that the European Union and International Diabetes Federation goal is below 6.5%; the panel's consensus was that an HbA1c of 7% or more should serve as a call to action, while noting that this goal is not appropriate or practical for some patients and that life expectancy and hypoglycaemia risk must be considered. The most appropriate target levels for blood glucose and HbA1c are stated not to have been systematically studied.
